title: Private Deployments: VPC & On-Prem Upgrade, Rollback, and Day-2 Operations Reference
author: Priya Rao
content:
Purpose

This page is a consolidated reference for deploying and operating Redwood Private (VPC and on-prem) installations. It covers recommended reference architectures, on-prem packaging, pre-deployment requirements, a detailed day-2 operations checklist, and deterministic upgrade and rollback procedures. Use this doc to align engineering, SRE, and customer engineering teams on validated operational steps and failure modes.

Scope and audience

- Scope: VPC-hosted Private control plane and on-prem packaged node deployments for Redwood Inference (CPU/GPU racks). Covers networking, packaging, observability, backups, upgrades, rollbacks, and common day-2 tasks.
- Audience: Customer Engineering, SREs, Platform Engineers, Professional Services.

Prerequisites and assumptions

- Customer has completed the network & security checklist in the customer requirements library.
- KMS/HSM integration planned for secrets and key management where required.
- Baseline monitoring (Prometheus + Grafana or equivalent) and log aggregation configured.
- Verified access to patch/maintenance windows for planned upgrades.

Reference architectures (summary)

1) VPC deployment (recommended for cloud customers)

- Control plane: Customer-managed control plane components optionally fronted by Redwood management plane during onboarding.
- Data plane: Dedicated GPU pools in private subnets; autoscaling groups for worker nodes.
- Networking: Private subnets, NAT for outbound, route tables per AZ, Transit Gateway for multi-region connectivity.
- Security: Private endpoint, private DNS, KMS integration, fine-grained IAM roles.

2) On-prem packaged deployment (recommended for air-gapped customers)

- Packaging: OCI images + tarball of prebuilt artifacts; installer bundle (k3s/kubernetes helm charts) with offline image registry.
- Hardware: GPU nodes (NVIDIA A100/A10 or equivalent) with host kernel >= 5.15, CUDA/driver matrix validated.
- Storage: NFS/CSI-backed persistent volumes for model artifacts and KV cache snapshots.
- Network: VLAN segmentation, BGP or static routing to customer fabric.

Packaging and distribution model

- Release artifacts: Signed OCI images, checksums for installer tarball, and a release manifest (SHA256).
- Offline installer: bundles/<version>/installer.tar.gz (includes images/, manifests/, scripts/)
- Version pinning: All YAML manifests declare imageDigest and appVersion. Customers are instructed to pin to these digests for predictable rollouts.

Pre-deployment checklist (network, security, infra)

- Networking
  - Allocate private subnets in each target AZ and define route tables.
  - Open required ports: 443 (control-plane), 9000-9010 (metrics & internal RPCs), 10250 (kubelet), and customer-specified ports for model-serving.
  - Verify NAT/egress rules for image pulls (if not using offline).
- Identity & Security
  - Configure KMS/HSM endpoints and test key wrapping/unwrapping.
  - Provision service accounts and RBAC roles per the minimum-privilege guide.
  - Enable audit logging and verify log forwarding (S3/GCS/ELK).
- Capacity Planning
  - Validate GPU inventory and expected token throughput. Use the capacity calculator (link to internal runbook) and include 20% headroom for burst.
- Observability
  - Deploy Prometheus, Grafana dashboards, and alerts defined in the observability standards.
  - Configure trace sampling for request-level tracing (1-5% by default).

Deployment procedure (high-level)

1. Validate prerequisites (network, KMS, storage).
2. Install control plane components (DB, control-plane services) in a canary AZ.
3. Deploy data plane worker nodes and attach to control plane.
4. Run post-installation validation tests (smoke tests, latency checks, model load test).
5. Promote to remaining AZs using rolling deployment policy.

Detailed Day-2 operations

Monitoring and alerts
- Key dashboards: token latency percentile, model load success rate, CPU/GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate, queue lengths per worker.
- SRE alert thresholds (examples):
  - P95 inference latency > 1.5x baseline for 5m -> P1 alert
  - GPU utilization > 95% sustained for 10m -> P2 alert (scale or investigate hot shards)
  - Model load failure rate > 2% in 10m -> P1 alert

Maintenance tasks
1) Backup and restore
  - Schedule daily snapshot of model-artifact storage and control-plane DB nightly to customer S3/GCS.
  - Quarterly full restore drill: restore to staging and run workload tests within SLA.
2) Security patching
  - Kernel and driver updates follow the maintenance window. For driver updates, always validate a single worker in canary first.
3) Scaling
  - Scale-up: add worker nodes to autoscaling groups and validate KV cache warm-up.
  - Scale-down: drain least-used nodes and ensure model shards redistributed without errors.

Upgrade procedure (recommended, step-by-step)

Goal: perform a zero-downtime rolling upgrade that preserves in-flight KV caches and model state where possible.

Pre-upgrade validation (day -3 to -1)
1. Verify backup integrity of control-plane DB and model artifacts.
2. Confirm release manifest digest and signatures.
3. Run smoke tests against the candidate version in a staging environment that mirrors production.
4. Notify customers/stakeholders and schedule maintenance window.

Canary upgrade (day 0)
1. Select a canary AZ or node pool (2-5% of production capacity).
2. Apply upgrade to canary control-plane components and associated worker nodes.
3. Run full validation suite (model load, inference latency, accuracy checks using saved prompt sets).
4. Monitor for 30-60 minutes for regressions. If regressions detected, proceed to rollback (see Rollback Procedure).

Rolling upgrade (day 0-1)
1. If canary is healthy, incrementally upgrade remaining AZs/node pools with a rolling window (configure maxUnavailable = 1 for control-plane stateful components where possible).
2. Use health checks and post-deployment probes to gate progression.
3. Keep previous release images available in the cluster in case immediate rollback is required.
4. After full rollout, run end-to-end smoke and regression checks and validate telemetry.

Post-upgrade validation (day +1)
1. Run production-quality workload tests against a test tenant or a traffic-shadowing setup.
2. Confirm SLOs (latency, error rate) are within thresholds for 24 hours before closing the maintenance window.

Rollback procedure (deterministic steps)

Rollback decision criteria
- Any sustained P1 alert tied to the new release during the canary or rolling phases.
- Regression in model quality (as measured by eval prompt-sets) that exceeds predefined thresholds.

Immediate rollback steps (when triggered)
1. Pause the rollout job and block further upgrades in the pipeline.
2. Revert control-plane images to previous digests by applying the previous manifest: kubectl apply -f manifests/release-<previous-digest>.yaml
3. For stateful control-plane components, follow the stateful rollback guide (restore DB snapshot if data-migration was applied).
4. For worker nodes, cordon and drain upgraded nodes and replace with nodes running the previous image, or use node-level image rollback procedure.
5. Validate service health and run critical smoke tests.
6. Open an incident, capture diagnostics (logs, traces, metrics), and notify stakeholders.

Rollback example CLI snippets
- Reapply previous manifest (control-plane):
  kubectl apply -f manifests/release-abcdef123456.yaml
- Drain a node and replace with previous image:
  kubectl cordon gpu-node-12
  kubectl drain gpu-node-12 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
  (reprovision node with image: registry.redwood.example/private-runtime:2027.11.01)

Safe rollback notes
- Data-format migrations: If the upgrade included irreversible data migrations, follow the data-migration rollback appendix and consider recovery to pre-upgrade cluster from DB snapshot.
- KV cache behavior: KV caches are best-effort preserved; if mismatch occurs, worker warm-start is required. Expect temporary CPU/GPU overhead as caches repopulate.

Troubleshooting and common failure modes

1) Control-plane not healthy after upgrade - Symptom: control-plane pods CrashLoopBackOff or failing readiness probes.
- Action: check logs (kubectl logs -n redwood control-plane-<pod>) for migration errors; if migration failed, restore DB snapshot and rollback release.

2) Model load failures on upgraded workers - Symptom: high model load failure rate and increased error traces.
- Action: verify driver/CUDA compatibility, check file permissions on model artifact storage, and compare expected model checksum with deployed artifacts.

3) Increased inference latency after rollout - Symptom: P95 and P99 latency regressions.
- Action: enable detailed profiling (perf/torch.profiler wrapper), collect traces, compare kernel selection and batching metrics between versions. Consider enabling fallback routing to a lower-cost model variant or increasing capacity temporarily.

- Secondary owner: Eng SRE (oncall rotation)
- Escalation: P1 -> oncall SRE -> Eng Platform lead -> CTO. Contact matrix in team wiki should be used for paging.

Appendices

A. Version compatibility matrix (example)
| Component | Minimum Version | Recommended Version | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Kubernetes | 1.24 | 1.26 | 1.26 preferred for CSI features |
| NVIDIA Driver | 525.x | 535.x | Match CUDA version matrix in packaging notes |
| CUDA | 11.8 | 12.1 | Validate with packaged runtime test |

B. Sample manifest snippet (image pinning)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: redwood-control-plane
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: control-plane
        image: registry.redwood.example/private-runtime@sha256:abcdef1234567890
        resources:
          limits:
            nvidia.com/gpu: 0

If you are preparing an upgrade for a customer, follow the steps in this document in order and raise any divergence during the pre-upgrade validation window. For questions or exceptions, open a customer ticket and include the pre-upgrade validation artifacts and test results.
